text: Little is known for certain about Robert Feke, and about 60 of his paintings survive, twelve of them signed and dated. In 1741 he moved to Boston and painted Isaac Royall and Family, a group portrait that borrows its composition from John Smibert's The Bermuda Group. Wollaston's work also influenced him. From then until 1750 he worked in Boston, Newport and Philadelphia, painting wealthy merchants and landowners. The latest record of him is from August 1751. Early biographers said he died in Barbados or Bermuda, but that has not been shown.

Roland Hipkins is especially noted for the work he made after the 1931 Hawke's Bay earthquake. He studied at the Bilston School of Art and served as a soldier in Malta and France before enrolling at the Royal College of Art in London. In 1922 he moved to Napier, New Zealand, one of several artists brought over to improve the teaching of art there. He taught at the Napier Technical College and helped found the Napier Society of Arts and Crafts. He married the Scottish artist Jenny Campbell, and the couple exhibited together. In 1930 they moved to Wellington.

Rudolf Stang grew up in the bar Zum Drachenfels, which his father ran in Düsseldorf and where local artists, poets and composers met. After his father died when he was nine, he was trained as a stonemason, and in 1845 he began attending the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf. After two years he made plates for small devotional images. His first full engraving was an Annunciation after Ernst Deger. From 1865 to 1874 he made several trips to Italy. The academies in Berlin and Munich named him a member for his engraving The Marriage of the Virgin.

Rutilio Manetti studied under Francesco Vanni and Ventura Salimbeni in Siena. Barocci influenced his earliest works. He is not documented in Rome, but he probably lived there between 1616 and 1621. From Caravaggio and his followers his paintings gained naturalism, solid forms and drama in lighting and gesture. He painted altarpieces, such as Saint Alexander Liberated by an Angel, and easel paintings, among them Samson and Delilah. After 1625 he also painted Caravaggesque gaming and concert scenes.

Seymour Joseph Guy trained and worked in London before he moved to New York in 1854. He had married Anna Maria Barber, the daughter of an engraver. In New York he became friends with John George Brown, and both began to paint genre pictures of children, probably inspired by their own. Guy eventually had nine. He was a founder of the American Watercolor Society and a member of the National Academy of Design and the Century Association.

Siegmund L'Allemand sat on the board that rejected Adolf Hitler's application to the Vienna academy in 1907. His uncle Fritz, a history painter, had given him his first lessons. He served as a battle painter in the Second Schleswig War in 1864, and two years later in the Third Italian War of Independence, where he took part in the Battle of Custoza. When his uncle died that year, Siegmund finished his unfinished paintings. After 1883 he was a professor at the Academy in Vienna.

Valeriano Bécquer often worked together with his younger brother, the poet Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer, on illustrations for magazines such as La Ilustración Española y Americana. Their father, a painter, gave Valeriano his first lessons before dying when the boy was eight. An uncle, Joaquín Domínguez Bécquer, taught him next, and he assisted in the uncle's workshop until 1853. In 1865 he received a government commission to paint festivals, costumes and customs from the Spanish regions, which meant years of travel. The Glorious Revolution withdrew the grant and left the project unfinished.

Walter Gay sailed to Paris in 1876 and became a pupil of Léon Bonnat. Sargent was a fellow student. Bonnat encouraged him to go to Spain, where he studied and copied Velázquez. Velázquez and the work of Mariano Fortuny influenced his brushwork, use of color and understanding of light. His uncle, the Boston painter Winckworth Allan Gay, had encouraged him to study in Paris. He was known for opulent interior scenes and for genre paintings of French peasants.

Abraham Solomon died in Biarritz of heart disease on 19 December 1862, the same day he was elected an Associate of the Royal Academy. His sister Rebecca and his youngest brother Simeon were artists too. His father, a Leghorn hat manufacturer, was one of the first Jews admitted to the freedom of the city of London. At thirteen Abraham became a pupil in Sass's school of art in Bloomsbury. His first exhibited work, Rabbi Expounding the Scriptures, appeared at the Society of British Artists in 1840.

Antonio Gherardi changed his name when he moved to Rome around 1656. His father, a middle-class craftsman, died when Antonio was eight. A patron, Monsignor Bulgarino Bulgarini, sponsored his trip to Rome and introduced him to Pier Francesco Mola and Pietro da Cortona. In Cortona's large workshops he learned both painting and stucco decoration. Cortona's influence was so strong that many of his first paintings were attributed to the old master. He joined the Accademia di San Luca in 1674.

Antonio Piccinni was left nearly deaf by an illness as an infant. He was born in Trani in Apulia but lived mainly in Naples and later Rome, where he won a stipend in 1872 to study at the Academy of Fine Arts. He painted mostly watercolors and was also an engraver. In 1877 the Regia Calcografia commissioned him to make a drawing after Andrea del Sarto's Madonna of the Harpies, to be turned into an engraving. He finished the charcoal sheet the next year. Francesco Di Bartolo won the competition to engrave it.

Caroline Watson was the only woman engraver to work as an independent engraver in 18th-century Britain. She studied under her father, the Irish engraver James Watson, who worked in mezzotint, and she became known for her stipple work and for reproductions of miniatures. In 1785 she dedicated a pair of small plates of Princesses Sophia and Mary to Queen Charlotte and was then appointed engraver to the Queen. She also engraved portraits of Catherine II of Russia and of William Woollett. Ill health slowed her career after 1810. She died at Pimlico in 1814.

Eduardo Zamacois y Zabala painted small canvases in the Academic style. He came from a family of writers, actors and musicians in Bilbao, and his father founded the Santiago de Vizcaya School of Humanities. When the school closed, the family moved to Madrid and in 1856 he enrolled at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, where he studied with Federico de Madrazo. In 1860 he went to Paris on Madrazo's recommendation and took Charles Gleyre's classes. The École des Beaux-Arts turned him down, so he found a position in Ernest Meissonier's workshop. He died young, at 29.

Emmanuel Viérin belongs to the Belgian Luminist current. He joined the Academy of Drawing and Painting in Courtrai at fifteen and later studied in Antwerp with the landscape painter Joseph Coosemans. In 1894 he spent six months in Algeria, where the very bright landscapes and the artists living in Biskra and Constantine left a mark. In 1896 he married Marguerite Bataille, and they had seven children. With his brother Joseph, an architect, he built Ter Wilgen, one of the first summer houses in Duinbergen on the Belgian coast. It is now a listed heritage building.

Ernest Duez admired Édouard Manet and owned paintings by Manet, Claude Monet, Edgar Degas and Berthe Morisot, yet his own palette was more subdued than that of most Impressionists. His style, between the conservative Salon and Impressionism, has been called juste milieu. He studied under Isidore Pils and first exhibited at the Salon in 1868 with Mater Dolorosa. Many of his landscapes and seaside scenes were inspired by the Normandy countryside around Villerville and Le Havre. His triptych Saint Cuthbert, shown at the Salon in 1879 and now in the Musée d'Orsay, is considered his greatest work.

François Chéreau was the first son of a carpenter in Blois, and his younger brother Jacques also became an engraver. He moved to Paris and studied with Gérard Audran and Pierre Drevet. He married Marguerite Caillou in 1714, and they had ten children. In 1718 he became engraver to the king's cabinet and was accepted by the Royal Academy after presenting a portrait of the young Louis de Boullongue. That year he also bought Audran's business, the Two Pillars of Gold, after the death of Audran's widow. He added the phrase with the King's privilege to his prints.

Friedrich van Hulsen, also called Frederik van Hulsen or Fredericus Hulsius, was a printmaker from Middelburg who worked in Frankfurt and Nuremberg. He became a pupil of Johann Theodor de Bry and was known for line engravings. His surname appears in several forms, among them Hulseen. He belonged to the Dutch Golden Age and lived from 1580 to 1665. He died in Frankfurt, far from his birthplace.

Georg Achen painted mainly landscapes in the 1880s, but from the 1890s he became one of Denmark's most popular portraitists, painting members of his family with special artistry. In 1890 he won the Thorvaldsen Medal for a portrait of his mother. Under the influence of Vilhelm Hammershøi, he also painted interiors with a dark female figure in pink, grey and brownish hues. The Dream Window, from 1903, shows a maid peering out of a window at Liselund Slot. He studied under Vilhelm Kyhn and at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. He died in Frederiksberg in 1912.

Giacomo Franco was the natural son of the painter and engraver Battista Franco and probably trained with him. He was probably born in Urbino, but all his known activity was in Venice. He illustrated books with etchings and engravings, such as Il ballarino by Fabritio Caroso in 1581 and the Venetian edition of Ovid's Metamorphoses in 1584. In 1590 he printed the first illustrated edition of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata, in Genoa. Its twenty plates were drawn by Bernardo Castello, who signed only two. He also made reproduction prints of paintings by Veronese.

At the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, Hendrik Adriaan Christiaan Dekker studied painting with Charles Rochussen and engraving with Johann Wilhelm Kaiser. He called himself Hein, but he signed his works HAC Dekker. He was a member of the Pulchri studio. He made lithographs after Jozef Israëls. He was born in Amsterdam in 1836 and died in Rheden in 1905, a Dutch painter and lithographer of the 19th century.

Ignacio Pinazo Camarlench came from a poor family in Valencia and worked as a silversmith, a tile painter and a decorator of fans. He later enrolled at the San Carlos Academy of Fine Arts and earned his living as a hatter. A painting he sold in 1873 paid for his first visit to Rome. When he came back in 1874 he gave up conventional historical themes for family subjects and scenes from daily life. That began his more intimate, Impressionist style. He returned to Rome in 1876 on a grant and stayed five years.

Jan Erasmus Quellinus came from a family of sculptors and painters, and his father Erasmus Quellinus the Younger trained him from 1649. In Rome from 1657 to 1659 he joined the Bentvueghels, an association of Dutch and Flemish artists, and got the bent name Seederboom, which means cedar tree. He then lived in Venice, where he was influenced by Veronese, and visited Naples. He worked mostly in his native Antwerp. For some time he was court painter to Emperor Leopold I in Vienna.

Józef Szermentowski painted landscapes under the influence of the Barbizon School. As a child he lived with his aunt, the abbess of the local monastery, where he first showed a talent for drawing. He studied at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw. After that he lived in Volyn and painted outdoors, and he also made decorations for the passenger ships of a steamship company. In 1860 a scholarship took him to Paris, where he became a friend of Cyprian Kamil Norwid. In 1868 he returned to Poland and set up a studio in the Tatras.

Marco Benefial was nineteen when an altarpiece of his was rejected for the Pantheon exhibition in Rome, and he was so angry that he displayed it in a pharmacist's window, to much commotion. In 1720 he protested against a rule of the Accademia di San Luca that only members could teach drawing. His appeal to Pope Clement XI had the rule revoked. The academy elected him at 57, but he soon denounced its members as mediocre and ignorant, and he was expelled in 1755. His painted figures are tangible, with luminous, warm colors.

Maurice Leloir was the son and pupil of the watercolorist Héloïse Suzanne Colin, and his brother Alexandre-Louis Leloir was a painter too. He first exhibited at the Salon des artistes français and later became its secretary. In 1907 he was the founding president of a society for the history of costume,. Around the 1890s he and his students flooded the picture book market with illustrations based on accurate costumes of the past. In 1884 Guy de Maupassant dedicated the short story Idylle to him.

Robert Thegerström worked for a year in his father's wholesale company in London before entering the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. His fellow students there included Ernst Josephson, Carl Larsson, Bruno Liljefors and Richard Bergh, who later formed the dissident Opponent movement. In 1880 he went to Paris and stayed in France for twelve years. Money made him a central figure in the Swedish artists' community there. He became good friends with Anders Zorn and went with him on a study trip to Spain and Morocco. His honeymoon with Elin Lamm was in Egypt.

Samuel Bough was the son of a shoemaker and a cook, and he grew up in relative poverty in Carlisle. He taught himself and was strongly influenced by the work of Turner. After an unsuccessful attempt to live as an artist in Carlisle he worked as a theatre scenery painter in Manchester and later in Glasgow. In 1851 he moved to Hamilton to take up landscape painting and worked there with Alexander Fraser. Next came Port Glasgow, where he worked on painting ships and harbours, and then Edinburgh in 1855. Following Turner's example, he became a skillful painter of seaports.

Samuel Pepys saw a flower piece by Simon Verelst in April 1669 and called it the finest thing he had ever seen, with dew drops on the leaves so real that he kept touching it to check. The Dutch art market collapsed in the late 1660s, and Simon, in difficult financial circumstances, moved from The Hague to London. His father and most of his siblings followed in 1668, and his father died that autumn. Simon married Ann Pember in 1684. Later he showed signs of mental illness.

Alexei Korzukhin grew up in a family of gold prospectors near Yekaterinburg and worked in a railway factory and the mint as a young man. In 1858 he entered the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts. In 1863 he joined the Revolt of the Fourteen, students who favored Realism and protested the Academy's insistence on the Classical style. They withdrew, and he accepted the designation Artist Second-Class. He then joined the Artel of Artists, a commune, until it disbanded in 1871. He also did portraits and religious works for the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour.

Alexey Bogolyubov's maternal grandfather was the philosopher Alexander Radishchev. He served in the Imperial Russian Navy and sailed with the fleet to many countries before he began to study at the Saint Petersburg Academy of Arts, where Ivan Aivazovsky greatly influenced him. From 1854 to 1860 he traveled around Europe. In Rome Alexander Ivanov convinced him to focus more on drawing, and in Düsseldorf he took classes from Andreas Achenbach. In Paris he admired the Barbizon painters, and Camille Corot and Charles-François Daubigny became good friends and collaborators.

Andreas Staub's most famous portrait, a lithograph of Clara Schumann, appeared on the 100 Deutschmark note between 1990 and 2001. Little is known of his life. He entered the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts at nineteen and soon exhibited watercolours. Around 1835 he made a series of lithographs of famous people, among them the pianist Sigismund Thalberg, the poet Nikolaus Lenau and the hydrotherapist Vincenz Prießnitz. He took his own life in Vienna at 32.

Antoš Frolka always dressed in Moravian costume and spoke in Moravian dialect. He came from a poor family in Kněždub and was partly taught by Joža Uprka. In 1914 he received a scholarship to study in Paris, but the outbreak of the First World War forced him to abandon it after six months. He was sent to the Eastern Front and then went through a severe crisis of creativity. His paintings are devoted to the small moments of everyday life and the folk culture of Moravia and Slovakia.

Bartolomeo Cesi came from a wealthy family in Bologna and first received a humanist education. His pious sobriety was influenced by his friendship with Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti. He worked in Rome with Scipione Pulzone and after returning in 1591 painted a series of frescoes on the Passion of Christ for the Carthusian monastery of San Girolamo in Bologna. In 1595 he completed a triptych for the Basilica of San Domenico. With Ludovico Carracci he campaigned successfully in 1599 to create a guild of painters in Bologna. He painted mainly religious subjects.

Carl Friedrich von Rumohr wrote about art history, cooking and farming, and he also drew and painted. He grew up on his family's estates in Holstein. At Göttingen he studied classical philology and history and took drawing lessons with Johann Dominik Fiorillo. In 1804 he converted to Catholicism together with the Riepenhausen brothers. A year later he went to Rome with Ludwig Tieck and the Riepenhausens, where he met German artists such as Joseph Anton Koch. He was also an art collector and a patron of artists.

Edith Halcombe was taught art by her father, William Swainson, who was a competent artist himself. She was born Edith Stanway Swainson in 1844, the daughter of his second wife Anne Grasby. In 1863 she married Arthur Halcombe at St James' Church in the Hutt. She was also a farmer. Her artworks, mainly landscapes of Manawatū, are in Te Papa, the Auckland Art Gallery and Puke Ariki.

Elias Muukka painted landscapes, mostly of rural Karelia and Turku, in the style of the Düsseldorf School. He studied in Helsinki, at the Düsseldorf academy and at the Académie Colarossi in Paris. He worked as a drawing instructor in Sordavala in Karelia and founded a private school for drawing and painting in Vaasa in 1886. From 1891 to 1918 he taught in Turku. He was one of the artists who joined Victor Westerholm at the artists' colony at Önningeby on the island of Åland in the late 1880s.

Emma Justine Farnsworth received her first camera as a gift in 1890 and was photographing seriously within a few months. The local amateur groups in Albany did not allow women, so she joined the Society of Amateur Photographers in New York City. Her photographs appeared in In Arcadia, a book of figure studies with classical verse, in 1892. They were exhibited at the World's Columbian Exposition in 1893. Before the end of the decade she had won almost 30 medals, and her work appeared often in Camera Notes, edited mainly by Alfred Stieglitz.

Ernst Klimt was the third of seven children of a gold engraver from Bohemia. At thirteen he became a student at the University of Applied Arts, where his older brother Gustav had been studying for a year. After the death of their teacher Ferdinand Laufberger in 1881, the two brothers and their school friend Franz Matsch founded the Künstler-Compagnie. Their company made curtains and ceiling paintings for theaters in Reichenberg, Karlsbad and Fiume, and frescoes for the new Burgtheater. Ernst's largest solo commissions were at Mondsee Castle and Peleș Castle in Romania.

Filippo Lauri often painted small figures into the landscapes of Claude Lorrain. His father, Balthasar Lauwers, was a Flemish landscape painter who had emigrated from Antwerp, and Filippo studied with him and then with his older brother Francesco. Afterwards he worked under his brother-in-law Angelo Caroselli. In 1654 he joined the Accademia di San Luca in Rome and later became its Principe, or director. He was prolific. He employed many engravers.

George Cuitt the Younger was the only son of the painter George Cuitt the Elder and followed his father's profession from his youth. A careful study of Piranesi's Roman Antiquities led him to take up etching. He went to Chester, where he taught drawing and published three sets of six etchings of old and picturesque buildings there around 1810. Later he retired to a house at Masham, near Richmond in Yorkshire, and published Yorkshire Abbeys. In 1848 he collected his etchings under the title Wanderings and Pencillings amongst the Ruins of Olden Times. He died at Masham in 1854.

Gijsbert d'Hondecoeter came from a family of painters. His father was Gillis d'Hondecoeter and his son was Melchior d'Hondecoeter. He mainly painted barnyard fowl, and some of his works are in the Rijksmuseum. He joined the Guild of St. Luke in Utrecht in 1629. When he died in 1653, his brother-in-law Jan Baptist Weenix continued the training of his son Melchior.

Giuseppe Valadier was expected to follow his father, a goldsmith, and did take over the family workshop, but he followed his own vocation from an early age. In 1775 he won a prize at the Accademia di San Luca with a design for the facade of San Salvatore in Lauro, and two years later, aged only 15, he won the Concorso Balestra for architecture. Before he was 20 he was appointed Architetto dei Sacri Palazzi. He also restored monuments, among them the Milvian Bridge and the Arch of Titus in Rome. He taught architecture at the Accademia di San Luca.

Henry Tonks trained as a surgeon before he became a painter. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1888 and taught anatomy at the London Hospital medical school. From 1888 he also studied art in the evenings at the Westminster School of Art under Frederick Brown. He exhibited with the New English Art Club from 1891 and became a member in 1895. When Brown became Slade Professor, Tonks started to teach at the Slade School. He became an influential teacher.

James Wilson Morrice is considered Canada's foremost modernist artist. He was born in Montreal and studied law in Toronto before he left for England to study painting. In 1891 he arrived in Paris, where he lived for most of his career. He began to paint small sketches on wooden panels, which he called pochades. Somerset Maugham knew him and had a character say that after you have seen his sketches you can never see Paris in the same way again.

Jan Damel came from Mitau, now Jelgava in Latvia, and studied art at Vilnius University under Jan Rustem and Franciszek Smuglewicz. He received his degree in 1809 and lived in Vilnius until he was accused of involvement in forgeries by Ignacy Julian Cejzyk. He was convicted and spent time in exile from 1820. He is considered one of the most prominent historical artists of the neoclassical genre in present-day Belarus. His works include paintings of the Kościuszko Uprising, Napoleon's army in Vilnius and the Battle of Vienna. Michał Kulesza was one of his students.

Jerzy Siemiginowski was of Armenian origin and was born in Lwów as Jerzy Szymonowicz. In 1677 he was entrusted to King John III Sobieski. He then probably spent a year or two in Paris before going to Rome, where he was trained by Lazzaro Baldi, Luigi Garzi and Carlo Maratta. In 1682 he won a contest at the Accademia di San Luca with two drawings of the Tower of Babel. After his return to Poland in 1684 the king ennobled him, and he took the name Eleuter, Greek for free, independent. He became court painter to Sobieski.

Franz von Matsch worked as a painter and sculptor in the Jugendstil style. With Gustav and Ernst Klimt he was a member of the Maler-Compagnie. He painted Achilles. It hangs in the Achillion Museum in Corfu. He was born in Vienna in 1861 and died there in 1942, and his full name was Franz Josef Karl Edler von Matsch. A 1981 catalog from the Museen der Stadt Wien calls him a Viennese painter of the turn of the century.

Louis-François Cassas became an apprentice draughtsman at fifteen in the Ponts et Chaussées office where his father worked. His godfather, the Marquis de Gallifet, owned the Château d'Azay-le-Ferron, where he was born. He studied in Tours and Paris before going to Rome in 1778, and then to Venice, Naples and Sicily to study ancient monuments. In 1782 a society of art lovers commissioned him to make illustrations of the antiquities on the east Adriatic coast, from Istria to southern Dalmatia. They were published as engravings in his two-volume Voyage pittoresque et historique de l'Istrie et de la Dalmatie.

Pierre-Charles Trémolières came from Cholet in Anjou and became an etcher and a decorative painter of interiors. Many of his works were once part of interior installations. Today they have been dismantled from those installations and remounted as movable paintings, which are shown in galleries. His subjects include The Birth of Venus and Sancho Panza Being Tossed in a Blanket. He died in Paris.

Prudent-Louis Leray was the son of a famous doctor from Nantes who distinguished himself during the cholera pandemic of 1832. He studied as a scholarship student at the college in Nantes and then entered the city school of fine arts. He became a pupil of Paul Delaroche and exhibited for the first time at the Salon of 1848. He excelled at genre paintings. He died at 58, four days after a stroke that struck him while he was painting in his workshop.
